verses.translation_literal: A psalm of David. Ascribe to YHWH, sons of gods, ascribe to YHWH glory and strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of David. And it begins with a summons thrown upward, past the hills and past the clouds, into the court of heaven: Give! You sons of the gods, you who stand about the throne, give to the LORD. Give him glory. Give him strength. Give, and give again.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with an imperative, hāvû, said twice, and the audience is not Israel but the heavenly court. 'Sons of gods' (bĕnê ʾēlîm) are the divine beings of the council that every neighbouring culture knew; in Canaanite thought the lesser gods stood around a high god, and here they are ordered to lay down their claims at YHWH's feet. Play it as a herald's command to equals who are no longer equals. The Targum says 'the company of angels'; Metzudat David agrees, while Ibn Ezra reads the stars, and Rashi and Meiri read the descendants of the patriarchs.

The KJV's 'O ye mighty' hides all of this: it takes ʾēlîm as 'strong ones' (the sense in Exod 15:15, 'the chiefs of Moab') and drops the 'sons of'. The ASV and YLT, 'sons of the mighty', keep the 'sons' but not the gods. Hāvû is a rare verb of giving, usually 'Come, give!' (Gen 29:21), and the KJV's plain 'give' is right, though 'ascribe' is the sense: to credit someone with what he already is. Note also that KJV counts the title as verse 0; in Hebrew it is part of verse 1.

philological_notes.note: 'Sons of gods', the divine beings of the heavenly council (compare Ps 89:7, bĕnê ʾēlîm, and bĕnê hāʾĕlōhîm in Job 1:6). The KJV 'mighty' reads ʾēlîm as 'strong ones'.
Imperative of yhb, 'give', used in summons ('Come, give', Gen 29:21). In the psalm it is repeated, a liturgical call to ascribe, to attribute what is due.

verses.translation_literal: Ascribe to YHWH the glory of his name; bow down to YHWH in the splendour of holiness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give to the LORD the glory that belongs to his name, and no less. Then bow. Bow low before the LORD, clothed in the radiance of what is holy.
verses.directors_commentary:
The summons moves from words to the body: first ascribe, then bow. Hishtaḥăwû is the full prostration of a subject before a king, and the voice in the line should drop with it. 'The glory of his name' means the weight and standing the name carries; Metzudat David says every one of his names speaks of his glory. Rashi counts eighteen mentions of the divine name in this psalm and says the Eighteen Blessings were set to match.

The KJV's 'the beauty of holiness' is the most famous mistranslation here. Hadrat-qōdesh is 'holy splendour' or 'holy array': either the sanctuary's majesty (so Meiri) or the vestments the worshippers wear, which the ASV and BBE render 'holy array' and 'holy robes'. 'Beauty' makes it sound like an aesthetic, when the word is about awe and display, the same hādār as in the 'majesty' of Lev 19:32, 'honour the face of an elder' (Radak). 'Worship' for hishtaḥăwû also loses the bodily act of bowing.

philological_notes.note: 'Splendour of holiness': the glory that belongs to a sacred place or the holy clothing worn in it. Not 'beauty of holiness' as an inward quality.
Hishtaphel of shḥh, 'to bow oneself down', prostration. Ibn Ezra reads it as a servant bowing to a master ready to do his orders.

verses.translation_literal: The voice of YHWH [is] over the waters; the God of the glory thunders; YHWH [is] over waters many.
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen. There is a voice, and it is the LORD's, and it is rolling over the waters. The God of glory thunders. The LORD, over the great waters, over the vast and heaving deep.
verses.directors_commentary:
From here the psalm is a storm. A voice, qôl, is heard seven times in the next verses, and in Hebrew qôl is both 'voice' and 'thunder' (as it still is in Exod 9:23, 'the LORD gave voices'). The storm is coming off the Mediterranean, which the ancient Near East treated as chaos itself: in Canaanite myth Baal the storm-god fights Sea. That is the point here, since the 'many waters' are the sea and the waters above the sky, and YHWH is simply over them. There is no fight and no rival.

The KJV's 'is upon the waters' fits; its 'thundereth' is right for hirʿîm, and the 'God of glory' keeps the definite article off ('the God of the glory'), the glory being the one the heavenly court was told to ascribe in verse 1. Rashi's Old French gloss explains hirʿîm; the rabbis hear Sinai in the line, Radak reads the sea. The three-fold 'YHWH' repeated with 'waters' is deliberate: the name falls like thunder claps.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of rʿm, 'to thunder' (also 1 Sam 7:10). The thunder is something God does with the voice, not a natural event in itself.
'Many waters', the standard idiom for the mighty deep, cosmic sea and flood (Ps 93:4; 18:17). In this storm psalm the waters are the sea beneath the sky and the heavens' waters.

verses.translation_literal: The voice of YHWH [is] in the power; the voice of YHWH [is] in the majesty.
verses.translation_dramatic: The voice of the LORD, and it is power. The voice of the LORD, and it is majesty. No word could be weightier; and none could be more splendid.
verses.directors_commentary:
The storm narrows to a drumbeat: qôl YHWH, qôl YHWH. The two lines are strict mirrors, 'in the power', 'in the majesty', and the actors should hit each noun. The definite article in each (baKōaḥ, behādār) is unusual: the Hebrew says 'in the power' and 'in the majesty', as if the voice were clothed in the very power and majesty that were demanded for it in verse 1. The sense is 'the' power and 'the' majesty that you know.

The KJV's 'is powerful' and 'is full of majesty' turn nouns into adjectives and lose the article; the literal 'with the power' is stronger. Rashi and Radak, hearing Sinai, say God shrank his voice to what Israel could bear ('according to the strength of each'); that is a rabbinic reading, not the plain sense. Ibn Ezra notes 'majesty' might be the mountains, which leads into the cedars of verse 5.

philological_notes.note: 'In the power', with the definite article, as a noun: the voice comes in the strength (not 'is strong'). Rashi hears a voice scaled to each hearer.

verses.translation_literal: Voice of YHWH, breaking cedars; and YHWH breaks in pieces the cedars of the Lebanon.
verses.translation_dramatic: The voice of the LORD is breaking cedars. Hear it: the great trunks give way with a crack like a sky splitting. The LORD breaks them, shatters them, the cedars of Lebanon, the proud ones, the ones that thought nothing could bring them down.
verses.directors_commentary:
Stage this as an ambush on the strongest thing in the landscape. The cedar of Lebanon was the ancient world's emblem of height, durability and royal wealth: Near Eastern kings felled it for temples and palaces, and Israel's own prophets use it as a figure for the proud and powerful. Here the thunder does what no axe-crew could. Metzudat David and Meiri both read the cedars as a figure for mighty men and kings; Rashi, quoting Samuel and Isaiah, takes them as the nations that fall when the LORD thunders. The poem works either way, and the actors should play both: real trees, real kings.

The Hebrew does something the KJV flattens. It first gives a participle, שֹׁבֵר, 'breaking', a continuous action that hangs in the air, and then switches to a different form of the same root, וַיְשַׁבֵּר, an intensive verb that means breaking into many pieces. The KJV's "breaketh … yea, breaketh" makes one repeated act; the Hebrew escalates from the crack to the splintering. The Targum hears the same two steps, with מַתְבַּר followed by וְתַבַּר. YLT's 'shivering' catches the force; BBE's passive recasts the sentence and hides the Lord as subject. The KJV's "yea" also adds an emphasis the Hebrew gets purely from repeating the divine name in the second half.

Note too that 'cedars' in the first half is bare, then specific and definite in the second: 'the cedars of the Lebanon'. The poem first names the kind of thing, then the place that everyone knew for it. Malbim hears the storm moving north to that forest. Metzudat Zion simply identifies Lebanon as a forest in the Land of Israel.

philological_notes.note: The same root as the participle שֹׁבֵר just before, but in the intensive (Piel) stem, which marks a breaking into pieces rather than a single fracture. This is my own grammatical observation; the Targum likewise uses two different verb forms (מַתְבַּר, וְתַבַּר) for the pair.

'The cedars of the Lebanon', with the article on Lebanon: the Lebanon range, known in the ancient world as the source of cedar timber. Meiri and Metzudat David take 'cedars' as a figure for kings and mighty men.

verses.translation_literal: And he makes them skip like a calf, Lebanon and Sirion like a son of wild oxen.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then the broken forest leaps. The LORD sets the cedars skipping like a calf let out into the sun, and Lebanon itself, and Sirion beside it, the old mountains, bounding like the young of the wild ox.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse where thunder becomes an earthquake you can see. The voice that snapped the cedars now shakes the ground under them, and the whole range rocks. Ibn Ezra notes that this is 'known from the working of thunder': anyone who has felt a storm roll through the mountains knows the ground shudder. Metzudat David glosses וַיַּרְקִידֵם as a motion of trembling, and Metzudat Zion as leaping and skipping. Play it as joy turned into terror, mountains behaving like frightened animals.

The KJV's "young unicorn" is the best-known mistake in the verse. The Hebrew רְאֵם is a wild ox, most likely the aurochs, a huge, fast, dangerous animal that is now extinct. In Assyrian this animal appears as rīmu, a word for the wild bull that decorates royal reliefs. The Septuagint's monokerōs, 'one-horned', is where the unicorn came from, and the KJV followed the Latin and Greek line. The ASV's 'young wild-ox' is right. The point of the image is the contrast of scale: a calf is small and skittish, a young aurochs is a calf with the power to match the mountains it is compared with. Meiri observes that a grown ox does not dance at all, but a young one skips and runs, so the poet chooses the young to show lightness of movement.

The verse also gives a mountain name that English readers miss. Sirion is the Sidonian name for Mount Hermon, the snowy peak at Lebanon's southern end; Rashi and Metzudat Zion say only that both are names of mountains. The pairing of Lebanon and Sirion stretches the storm from the northern forest to Israel's own northern border, so the whole north rocks.

philological_notes.note: A causative (Hiphil) of 'to skip, leap': 'he made them skip', with the suffix pointing back to the cedars. The LORD is the one who sets them dancing; they do not move on their own. Metzudat Zion glosses it as springing and skipping.

Literally 'son of wild oxen', meaning one of that kind, as 'son of she-asses' means a young ass. Ibn Ezra and Meiri read it just so, as in 'ben athonot'; Metzudat Zion reads it as a young animal. This is not a unicorn: my own reading is that רְאֵם is the wild ox (aurochs), also known from Akkadian rīmu, and that 'unicorn' in the KJV goes back to the Septuagint's one-horned rendering.
Sirion: a name for Mount Hermon (Deut 3:9 gives it as the Sidonian name). The commentaries in the packet say only that Lebanon and Sirion are mountain names.

verses.translation_literal: The voice of YHWH [is] hewing flames of fire.
verses.translation_dramatic: The voice of the LORD. It hews. It cuts out blades of flame from the dark, and the lightning falls.
verses.directors_commentary:
A verse of five words, and the shortest of the seven voices: the pause around it is the lightning. Ḥōṣēv is a stoneworker's word, to hew or quarry (as the pillars of Wisdom's house are hewn in Prov 9:1), and God is shown cutting flames out of the sky like blocks. Radak and Ibn Ezra take the flames as lightning, and Ibn Ezra gives the image of arrows from the Most High's voice. Rashi, in the old tradition, hears the Ten Commandments cut in fire from his mouth into the tablets.

The KJV 'divideth the flames of fire' is a soft rendering: it imagines forked lightning splitting, but the Hebrew says 'hews', a verb of violence and of carving. The BBE's 'flames of fire are seen' loses the verb entirely. Keep the carving; it is the moment the voice becomes visible.

philological_notes.note: To hew, quarry or cut out, a mason's and miner's verb (Prov 9:1; Deut 8:9). Of lightning it pictures God cutting fire out of the sky; the KJV 'divideth' is a guess at forked lightning.

verses.translation_literal: The voice of YHWH makes writhe [the] wilderness; YHWH makes writhe the wilderness of Kadesh.
verses.translation_dramatic: The voice of the LORD, and the wilderness writhes; the LORD makes the wilderness of Kadesh writhe, as a woman writhes in labour, and the sand and stone shudder under it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The storm sweeps from the north, over Lebanon, down to the empty land. Yāḥîl is the verb of labour pains and trembling: Rashi ties it to 'pain like a woman in labour' (Jer 6:24), and Radak to 'you will cause pain to every good field with stones' (2 Kgs 3:19). So the desert is not just shaken; it is in agony. The Hebrew repeats the verb and the place name, so the line is a pounding pair: wilderness, wilderness of Kadesh.

The KJV 'shaketh' loses the birth-pains the root carries, and it makes the rumble of an earthquake out of what is an animate pain. The identification of Kadesh is open: the oasis in the Negev (the packet's reading, and Rashi's Sinai-wilderness tradition) is far south, while a Kadesh on the Orontes river in the north would fit the storm's path from Lebanon. A wilderness is the place of no one: the thunder reaches even where nobody can hear it.

philological_notes.note: From ḥwl/ḥyl, 'to writhe, whirl, be in labour pains': the desert is racked like a woman in labour. The KJV 'shaketh' flattens it.

verses.translation_literal: The voice of YHWH brings to labour does, and strips bare forests; and in his temple all of it [is] saying: Glory!
verses.translation_dramatic: The voice of the LORD, and the does are seized and bring forth in terror; and the forests are laid bare, stripped to the bone. But in his temple, in that one place, everything cries out one word: Glory!
verses.directors_commentary:
The storm ends in the one place it does not touch. Outside, the thunder makes the wild does drop their young early (a doe's labour is hard and fear brings it on, says Ibn Ezra) and rips the leaves and branches from the forest, leaving it bare. Then the cut: 'in his temple', where the same sound is heard as liturgy, and the whole assembly, or everything in it, says 'Glory!' Metzudat David says everyone who enters the sanctuary says, 'now his glory is seen'; Malbim says the sons of gods bowed there.

The KJV's 'discovereth the forests' is archaic ('discover' meaning to uncover); the Hebrew is 'strips bare'. 'Maketh the hinds to calve' follows the animal reading, but it is not certain: the Radak passage cites Lowth's view that ʾayyālôt are 'terebinths' (oaks), which suits the parallel with forests and is the YLT's 'oaks'. And 'doth every one speak of his glory' adds 'his' and 'of' that the Hebrew lacks: it says simply 'Glory!'. The final word is the cry, the answer to the opening summons of verse 1.

philological_notes.note: 'Brings does to labour', or if the noun is ʾēlôt 'terebinths', 'makes oaks writhe'. The labour reading is the traditional one; the tree reading answers the 'forests' of the next line.
To strip bare (Gen 30:37, the peeled rods). Of forests it is the stripping of leaves and bark. The KJV 'discovereth' means 'uncovers' in old English.
'Temple' or palace; of God it is either the sanctuary in Jerusalem or the heavenly palace. Ibn Ezra lists both readings.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH sat to the Flood, and YHWH sits [as] king for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD sat enthroned over the Flood, as he sat then, so he sits now. The LORD is seated as king, and he is king for ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the noise, a seated figure. The verb is the same twice, yāshav and wayyēshev, but its tense moves from the past ('sat', at the Flood) to the lasting present ('sits as king for ever'). The Flood, mabbûl, is the one great water that the Bible gives a proper noun, the time when the cosmic waters really did rise, and this verse says that even then God was not swept off: he was on the throne. The storm that has just torn through Lebanon is small beside that; and God's rule is older than any storm.

The KJV 'sitteth upon the flood' is a standard translation, though it erases the tense change and the Genesis link; the ASV 'sat as King at the Flood' is closer. Hebrew lamma-būl has a lāmed that means 'to' or 'at': 'to the Flood', with the sense of 'for the Flood' or 'enthroned over'. The rabbinic tradition (Rashi, Radak, the Targum) hears the Noah story: Rashi has the nations ask Balaam, 'is this a flood?' and he answers, God has sworn never to bring one.

philological_notes.note: 'The Flood', mabbûl, found only here and in Genesis 6-11. The lāmed can mean 'at' or 'over'; either way it points to Noah's flood and God enthroned above it.
'Sat', and then wayyēshev: the same verb in the past and the open-ended present, 'sat … sits'. The seat is a throne.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH strength to his people will give; YHWH will bless his people with peace.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD will give strength to his people. The LORD will bless his people with peace. And the thunder falls quiet.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice that broke cedars ends in a blessing. The psalm began by telling heaven to give strength (ʿōz) to YHWH, and it ends with YHWH giving that same word, ʿōz, to his people: the strength flows back down. 'Peace' (shālôm) is the last word, and after seven claps of thunder it is meant to land softly; the actors should let the sound die away. The last line is also the priestly blessing's cadence (Num 6:24-26), the LORD blessing his people.

The KJV is sound here, 'will give strength', 'will bless with peace', though its future 'will' is an interpretation: the Hebrew imperfect can also be a habit, 'gives', 'blesses'. Radak and Meiri read it as the messianic end of war; Ibn Ezra as prayer or inspiration that God give strength in thunderstorms. Metzudat David reads the plain verse as it stands. The BBE's 'the blessing of peace' adds a noun.

philological_notes.note: 'Strength', the same word asked of the sons of gods in verse 1 ('glory and strength'); here it comes back as God's gift. Radak, by a rabbinic play, hears it as Torah.
'With peace': shālôm is wholeness and well-being, not only the absence of war; the final word of the psalm.
